Assigning new documents and topic mixtures

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/assigning-topics.Rmd
assigning-topics.Rmd

A fitted topic model is a set of topic centers in an embedding space, and it can be used beyond the texts it was fitted on. New texts collected after the analysis can be placed in the existing topics, so that a coding scheme derived from one sample is applied to the next without refitting it. A text that lies between two topics can be described by its degree of membership in each, rather than by one topic. A document made of several units, such as a session of messages or an abstract of several sentences, can be described by the mixture of topics among its units. And when the categories are known in advance, they can be supplied as seeds and the texts assigned to them.

This guide shows these four uses on the feedback messages. It also states how assigning a new text differs from the assignment made during fitting, and how often the two disagree.

library(sbert)
#> sbert 0.5.14: Sentence-BERT embeddings and topic models in R.
#>   14 pinned models (see models()); default: all-MiniLM-L6-v2.
#>   A model is downloaded only on request, once, and verified by SHA-256.

Data

The first 500 of the 600 distinct feedback messages with bundled embeddings are used to fit the model, and the last 100 are held out as new messages. head() and tail() split the data frame and the embedding matrix in the same way, so row i of each part still embeds message i of that part.

  • translation: the English text of each message; the modeled text.
  • n: the number of times the message occurs in the full corpus.
  • feedback_embeddings: one 384-dimensional all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embedding per message.
corpus <- head(dedupe(feedback_translations, column = "translation"), 600)
training <- head(corpus, 500)
training_embeddings <- head(feedback_embeddings, 500)
held_out <- tail(corpus, 100)
held_out_embeddings <- tail(feedback_embeddings, 100)

The model is fitted with six topics on the training messages:

topic_model <- topics(training, n_topics = 6, column = "translation",
                      embeddings = training_embeddings)
topic_sizes(topic_model)
#>   topic                                                       label n_documents
#> 1     1   Where is the cow and the cake? Choose all the pictures...         142
#> 2     2          What does “all the ones between the dog and the...         126
#> 3     3            All the ones between the cat and the strawberry.         109
#> 4     4             Which one comes right after the eighth picture?          51
#> 5     5 Are you sure you have fewer pictures in the red box than...          44
#> 6     6               It’s a person, has a hat, and isn’t standing.          28
#>   proportion
#> 1      0.284
#> 2      0.252
#> 3      0.218
#> 4      0.102
#> 5      0.088
#> 6      0.056

The six topics hold 142, 126, 109, 51, 44 and 28 of the 500 messages: guiding questions with an instruction, questions about meaning, short hints, questions about the position of a picture, corrections, and negations.

Which topic does a new message belong to?

predict() assigns each new text to the topic whose center is most similar to it by cosine similarity. The model is not changed. text takes a character vector, so with() passes the column of the held-out data frame; with a downloaded model, predict() would encode the texts itself, and here the bundled embeddings are passed:

predicted <- with(held_out, predict(topic_model, translation,
                                    embeddings = held_out_embeddings))
head(predicted, 4)
#>   document_id document_name
#> 1           1              
#> 2           2              
#> 3           3              
#> 4           4              
#>                                                                                      text
#> 1          Where is the leaf and the watermelon? Choose the picture that is between them.
#> 2      Where is the lollipop and the tram? Choose all the pictures that are between them.
#> 3                               All the pictures between the mosquito and the teddy bear.
#> 4 Where is the cucumber and the ice cream? Choose all the pictures that are between them.
#>   topic                                                     label distance
#> 1     1 Where is the cow and the cake? Choose all the pictures...    0.247
#> 2     1 Where is the cow and the cake? Choose all the pictures...    0.328
#> 3     1 Where is the cow and the cake? Choose all the pictures...    0.367
#> 4     1 Where is the cow and the cake? Choose all the pictures...    0.269
with(predicted, table(label))
#> label
#>            All the ones between the cat and the strawberry. 
#>                                                          16 
#> Are you sure you have fewer pictures in the red box than... 
#>                                                           6 
#>               It’s a person, has a hat, and isn’t standing. 
#>                                                           3 
#>          What does “all the ones between the dog and the... 
#>                                                          29 
#>   Where is the cow and the cake? Choose all the pictures... 
#>                                                          40 
#>             Which one comes right after the eighth picture? 
#>                                                           6

The result has one row per new message, with its topic, the topic’s label, and distance, the cosine distance to the assigned center. The 100 new messages fall into all six topics, most often the guiding questions (40) and the questions about meaning (29). The distance tells how well a new message fits its topic:

with(predicted, summary(distance))
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   0.174   0.282   0.335   0.342   0.378   0.655
with(as.data.frame(topic_model), summary(distance))
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   0.114   0.251   0.304   0.328   0.377   0.753

The new messages lie at a median distance of 0.335 from their centers, against 0.304 for the training messages, so the held-out messages fit the topics almost as well as the messages that formed them. A new message at a large distance (the largest here is 0.655) is one the topics do not describe well, and a cluster of such messages is a sign that the new data contain a kind of text the model has not seen.

Does predict() reproduce the fitted topics?

Not exactly. topics() forms the topics with k-means (Lloyd, 1982), which assigns each embedding to the nearest center by Euclidean distance, and its centers are the means of the (unit-length) embeddings of each topic, which are shorter than unit length. predict() assigns by cosine similarity to the centers normalized to unit length. The two rules agree for nearly every text but can differ for a text that lies on the boundary between two topics. Predicting the training messages and cross-tabulating the result against their fitted topics shows how often:

repredicted <- with(training, predict(topic_model, translation,
                                      embeddings = training_embeddings))
assignments <- merge(as.data.frame(topic_model), repredicted,
                     by = "document_id", suffixes = c("_fit", "_predict"))
with(assignments, table(topic_fit, topic_predict))
#>          topic_predict
#> topic_fit   1   2   3   4   5   6
#>         1 142   0   0   0   0   0
#>         2   0 124   0   0   0   2
#>         3   0   0 109   0   0   0
#>         4   0   0   0  50   1   0
#>         5   0   0   0   0  44   0
#>         6   0   0   0   0   0  28

Three of the 500 messages change topic, all of them far from every center:

subset(assignments, topic_fit != topic_predict,
       select = c(text_fit, topic_fit, topic_predict, distance_predict))
#>                                                                             text_fit
#> 8                                              If it’s sitting, what does that mean?
#> 70  Having a beak means having a hard, pointy thing on your head instead of a mouth.
#> 125                       Train cars with the same number must be on the same train.
#>     topic_fit topic_predict distance_predict
#> 8           2             6            0.540
#> 70          2             6            0.621
#> 125         4             5            0.658

Each of the three lies more than 0.5 from its nearest center, where the two rules can rank two centers differently. For new texts the cosine rule is the one applied, so a topic count from predict() can differ from the fitted count by such boundary cases. For the fitted messages, use the fitted topics (as.data.frame(topic_model) or topic_sizes()).

How strongly does a message belong to each topic?

A hard assignment hides how close a message came to another topic. topic_membership() gives every message a probability for every topic, computed from its cosine distances to all centers as in fuzzy c-means (Bezdek, 1981), and ranks the topics within each message:

membership <- topic_membership(topic_model)
head(membership, 6)
#>   document_id topic probability rank
#> 1           1     2     0.87862    1
#> 2           1     5     0.09172    2
#> 3           1     4     0.02165    3
#> 4           1     3     0.00397    4
#> 5           1     6     0.00296    5
#> 6           1     1     0.00109    6

The probabilities sum to one within each message. Their spread is set by sharpness, the fuzzifier: the closer it is to 1, the crisper the memberships. The default, 1.15, is low because distances between sentence embeddings are concentrated, and the textbook value of 2 pulls every message toward an even split. The probability of each message’s strongest topic under both values:

with(subset(membership, rank == 1), summary(probability))
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   0.314   0.984   0.999   0.959   1.000   1.000
with(subset(topic_membership(topic_model, sharpness = 2), rank == 1),
     summary(probability))
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   0.197   0.368   0.462   0.467   0.543   0.867

With the default, the median message gives 0.999 of its membership to one topic, and the least decided message 0.314. With sharpness = 2 the median falls to 0.462. The ranking of the topics within a message does not depend on sharpness; the magnitudes do, so they are compared across messages at one fixed value. The messages whose strongest membership is low are the ones to read when the boundary between two topics matters.

New messages take their embeddings through embeddings =. Their strongest topic is the topic predict() assigns:

new_membership <- topic_membership(topic_model, embeddings = held_out_embeddings)
strongest <- merge(subset(new_membership, rank == 1), predicted,
                   by = "document_id", suffixes = c("_membership", "_predict"))
with(strongest, table(topic_membership, topic_predict))
#>                 topic_predict
#> topic_membership  1  2  3  4  5  6
#>                1 40  0  0  0  0  0
#>                2  0 29  0  0  0  0
#>                3  0  0 16  0  0  0
#>                4  0  0  0  6  0  0
#>                5  0  0  0  0  6  0
#>                6  0  0  0  0  0  3

What mix of topics does a document contain?

When a document is made of several units, topic_gamma() assigns every unit to a topic and reports the share of each topic among the document’s units. The feedback data do not record which messages a learner saw together, so for illustration the 100 held-out messages are grouped, in their order, into ten blocks of ten that stand in for sessions. topic_gamma() accepts a data frame with a document_id and a text column, one row per unit, with one embedding row per unit:

sessions <- with(held_out, data.frame(document_id = rep(seq_len(10), each = 10),
                                      text = translation))
topic_gamma(topic_model, sessions, embeddings = held_out_embeddings, top = 2)
#>    document_id rank topic gamma n_segments
#> 1            1    1     1   0.9         10
#> 2            1    2     2   0.1         10
#> 3            2    1     1   0.8         10
#> 4            2    2     2   0.2         10
#> 5            3    1     2   0.4         10
#> 6            3    2     1   0.3         10
#> 7            4    1     2   0.5         10
#> 8            4    2     1   0.4         10
#> 9            5    1     1   0.3         10
#> 10           5    2     2   0.3         10
#> 11           6    1     1   0.3         10
#> 12           6    2     4   0.3         10
#> 13           7    1     1   0.4         10
#> 14           7    2     2   0.3         10
#> 15           8    1     2   0.4         10
#> 16           8    2     3   0.4         10
#> 17           9    1     2   0.4         10
#> 18           9    2     3   0.4         10
#> 19          10    1     1   0.3         10
#> 20          10    2     2   0.2         10

With top = 2, each block lists its two largest topic shares. The first two blocks are dominated by guiding questions (0.9 and 0.8 of their messages); in each later block no kind of feedback exceeds half of the messages. Without top, every topic of every document is listed, and the shares of a document sum to one.

The usual case is a document split into sentences. The example below is invented to show the steps: three short documents, each mixing pets and finance, with made-up two-dimensional embeddings, one row per sentence, in which the first coordinate stands for pets and the second for finance. segment() shows the sentences the embeddings must follow:

documents <- c("Cats chase mice. Stocks and bonds trade.",
               "Dogs chase balls. Markets price shares.",
               "Kittens nap in the sun. Banks report profit. Puppies play.")
segment(documents, level = "sentence")
#>   document_id document_name segment                    text
#> 1           1                     1        Cats chase mice.
#> 2           1                     2 Stocks and bonds trade.
#> 3           2                     1       Dogs chase balls.
#> 4           2                     2   Markets price shares.
#> 5           3                     1 Kittens nap in the sun.
#> 6           3                     2    Banks report profit.
#> 7           3                     3           Puppies play.
sentence_embeddings <- rbind(c(1, 0), c(0, 1), c(0.9, 0.1), c(0.1, 0.9),
                             c(0.95, 0.05), c(0.05, 0.95), c(0.8, 0.2))

A model fitted with segment = "sentence" models the sentences and keeps, for each, the document it came from, so topic_gamma() needs no text:

sentence_model <- topics(documents, n_topics = 2, segment = "sentence",
                         embeddings = sentence_embeddings)
topic_gamma(sentence_model)
#>   document_id topic gamma n_segments
#> 1           1     1 0.500          2
#> 2           1     2 0.500          2
#> 3           2     1 0.500          2
#> 4           2     2 0.500          2
#> 5           3     1 0.667          3
#> 6           3     2 0.333          3
topic_sizes(sentence_model, by = "document")
#>   topic                label n_documents proportion
#> 1     1    Dogs chase balls.           3          1
#> 2     2 Banks report profit.           3          1

Each of the first two documents is half pets and half finance; the third, with two sentences about pets and one about finance, is two thirds pets. topic_sizes(by = "document") counts the documents with at least one sentence in a topic, so every document is counted in both topics here. To place new documents in a sentence-level model, pass them to topic_gamma(model, text) or predict(model, text): they are split with the fitted segmentation settings, and the embeddings must follow the same sentences. Choosing and tuning the segmentation is covered in Segmenting long documents.

Can topics be defined in advance?

When the categories are known before the analysis, they can be given to topics() as seeds, one per category. Each seed is a text, such as a short description of the category, whose embedding becomes the center of its topic. With fixed_seeds = TRUE the centers stay where the seeds put them and every text joins its nearest seed: a zero-shot classification into the given categories, with no topics discovered. With a downloaded model, the seed descriptions are encoded with the texts; this chunk is not run here:

model_download()
zero_shot <- topics(training, n_topics = 3, column = "translation",
                    seeds = c(meaning = "What does this phrase mean?",
                              correction = "There should be more in the red box.",
                              negation = "It is not a person."),
                    fixed_seeds = TRUE)

Without a model, a seed can be given a prototype embedding instead: the mean embedding of a few texts that clearly belong to the category. Here five kinds of feedback are identified by how their messages begin or what they contain, and each prototype is the column mean of the matching rows of the training embeddings. subset() selects the rows of the matrix:

prototype <- function(pattern) {
  with(training, colMeans(subset(training_embeddings, grepl(pattern, translation))))
}
seed_embeddings <- rbind(prototype("^Where is"), prototype("^All the ones between"),
                         prototype("^What does"), prototype("^There should be"),
                         prototype("not a person"))
dim(seed_embeddings)
#> [1]   5 384

The names of seeds become the labels of the topics, and seed_embeddings supplies their vectors in the same order:

feedback_seeds <- c(instruction = "Guiding question and instruction",
                    hint = "Short hint", meaning = "Question about meaning",
                    correction = "Correction", negation = "Negation")
zero_shot <- topics(training, n_topics = 5, column = "translation",
                    embeddings = training_embeddings, seeds = feedback_seeds,
                    seed_embeddings = seed_embeddings, fixed_seeds = TRUE)
topic_sizes(zero_shot)
#>   topic       label n_documents proportion
#> 1     1 instruction         183      0.366
#> 2     2        hint         121      0.242
#> 3     3     meaning         130      0.260
#> 4     4  correction          37      0.074
#> 5     5    negation          29      0.058

Every message is placed in one of the five categories, the instructions being the largest (183 messages). The cross-tabulation against the unsupervised six-topic model shows where the two agree:

comparison <- merge(as.data.frame(topic_model), as.data.frame(zero_shot),
                    by = "document_id", suffixes = c("_unsupervised", "_seeded"))
with(comparison, table(topic_unsupervised, topic_seeded))
#>                   topic_seeded
#> topic_unsupervised   1   2   3   4   5
#>                  1 141   1   0   0   0
#>                  2   0   1 122   1   2
#>                  3   0 108   1   0   0
#>                  4  33  10   6   2   0
#>                  5   9   1   0  34   0
#>                  6   0   0   1   0  27

Five of the six unsupervised topics map onto one category each: 141 of 142 guiding questions, 122 of 126 questions about meaning, 108 of 109 hints, 34 of 44 corrections and 27 of 28 negations. The sixth unsupervised topic, the 51 questions about the position of a picture, had no seed, and a zero-shot classification cannot create a category: its messages are spread over instructions (33), hints (10), questions about meaning (6) and corrections (2). Fixed seeds therefore suit a coding scheme that is complete; a kind of text without a seed is forced into the nearest one, and only its distance shows that it fits badly.

With fixed_seeds = FALSE (the default), the seeds are starting centers: k-means moves them, and n_topics may exceed the number of seeds, the remaining topics being found in the data. This guides the topics toward known categories while leaving room for new ones:

guided <- topics(training, n_topics = 6, column = "translation",
                 embeddings = training_embeddings, seeds = feedback_seeds,
                 seed_embeddings = seed_embeddings)
topic_sizes(guided)
#>   topic                      label n_documents proportion
#> 1     1                instruction         185      0.370
#> 2     2                       hint         117      0.234
#> 3     3                    meaning         130      0.260
#> 4     4                 correction          36      0.072
#> 5     5                   negation          30      0.060
#> 6     6 That was first-class work!           2      0.004

The five seeded topics keep their seeds’ labels and stay close to the zero-shot sizes, and the one free topic holds only 2 messages, so it did not recover the 51 questions about position. Seeds guide the analysis toward the given categories; whether the data hold others is still answered by an unsupervised fit.

When to use which

Question Verb
Which topic does a new text belong to? predict(model, text)
How well does it fit? the distance column of predict()
How strongly does a text belong to each topic? topic_membership(sharpness = )
What mix of topics is in a document? topic_gamma(), topic_gamma(top = )
How many documents touch each topic? topic_sizes(by = "document")
Classify into known categories topics(seeds = , fixed_seeds = TRUE)
Guide topics toward known categories topics(seeds = )

How the topics were chosen and described is covered in Choosing the number of topics and the granularity and Describing and naming topics; the complete analysis is in Semantic topic modeling with Sentence-BERT.

References

Bezdek, J. C. (1981). Pattern recognition with fuzzy objective function algorithms. Plenum Press. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-0450-1

Lloyd, S. P. (1982). Least squares quantization in PCM. IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 28(2), 129–137. https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.1982.1056489
